title: What Even Is Machine Learning?

character.name: The Pattern Seer
character.tagline: I don't write the rules. I let the data whisper them to me.

oneLiner: The big idea: instead of coding rules by hand, you let a model learn patterns from examples.
analogy: Traditional programming is a strict recipe: 'IF tomato AND basil THEN pizza.' Machine learning is raising a toddler on a thousand photos of pizza until they just KNOW it's pizza — even a weird one they've never seen. You never wrote the rule 'melted cheese + round'; the toddler inferred it. Supervised learning is showing labeled flashcards ('this is a cat'), unsupervised is dumping toys on the floor and letting them sort into piles, and reinforcement is training a puppy with treats for good moves.
objectives: Contrast rule-based programming with learning from data.
Distinguish supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning.
Know when ML is the right tool (and when a plain rule is better).
keyConcepts: ML learns patterns from examples instead of relying on hand-written rules — great when rules are too complex or unknown.
Supervised learning uses labeled data (inputs + correct answers) to predict labels for new inputs.
Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data (e.g. clustering, dimensionality reduction).
Reinforcement learning learns by trial and error, maximizing a reward signal over time.
Training is the learning phase; inference is using the trained model to make predictions.
If a simple deterministic rule solves the problem reliably, you often don't need ML at all.

keyTerms.plain: Learning from flashcards with the answers on the back.
Sorting a pile of stuff into groups with no labels given.
Learning by trial, error, and treats (rewards).
The practice phase where the model learns from data.
Game time — using the trained model to make predictions.

scenarios.scenario: You have thousands of customer reviews and want to automatically group them into themes, but you have no predefined categories or labels.
scenarios.question: Which type of learning fits best?

options.label: No learning — write IF/ELSE rules for every theme

scenarios.explanation: With no labels and a goal of discovering structure/groups, unsupervised clustering is the natural fit. Supervised learning would require labeled examples up front.

scenarios.scenario: A task needs to decide whether a number is even or odd.
scenarios.question: Should you train an ML model for this?

options.label: No — a trivial deterministic rule (check the last bit) is simpler and perfect
Yes, train a deep neural network on millions of examples
Yes, but only with a GPU cluster

scenarios.explanation: When a simple exact rule exists, use it. ML shines for problems too complex or fuzzy to hand-code, not for things a one-line rule already nails.

quiz.question: What fundamentally distinguishes machine learning from traditional programming?
options: ML runs only on GPUs
ML learns patterns from data instead of following explicitly hand-coded rules
ML never makes mistakes
ML doesn't use code
quiz.answer: ML learns patterns from data instead of following explicitly hand-coded rules
quiz.explanation: Instead of a human specifying every rule, ML infers patterns from examples — useful when rules are unknown or too complex.

quiz.question: Supervised learning requires:
options: Unlabeled data only
Labeled examples (inputs paired with correct outputs)
A reward signal
No data at all
quiz.answer: Labeled examples (inputs paired with correct outputs)
quiz.explanation: Supervised learning trains on inputs with known correct answers so it can predict labels for new inputs.

quiz.question: Which is an example of reinforcement learning?
options: Grouping photos with no labels
An agent learning to play a game by earning rewards for good moves
Predicting house prices from labeled sales
Cleaning a CSV file
quiz.answer: An agent learning to play a game by earning rewards for good moves
quiz.explanation: RL learns through trial and error guided by a reward signal, improving its policy over time.

quiz.question: What is 'inference'?
options: The phase where the model learns from data
Using a trained model to make predictions on new inputs
Deleting the training set
Labeling data by hand
quiz.answer: Using a trained model to make predictions on new inputs
quiz.explanation: Training is learning; inference is applying the trained model to produce predictions.

quiz.question: When is ML often NOT the right tool?
options: When a reliable simple rule already solves the problem exactly
When the problem is fuzzy and hard to specify
When you have lots of labeled examples
When patterns are too complex to hand-code
quiz.answer: When a reliable simple rule already solves the problem exactly
quiz.explanation: If a deterministic rule works, it's simpler, cheaper, and more reliable than ML. Save ML for genuinely complex or fuzzy problems.
